title: Closing Entries in Accounting: A Step-by-Step Guide (October 2026)
summary: Master closing entries in accounting with step-by-step instructions, real journal entry examples, and tips for a faster month-end close. October 2026.
body_markdown:
Closing entries sit at the end of the accounting cycle, and they're easy to rush through because the financial statements are already done by that point. But skipping steps or closing in the wrong order is where balances carry forward by mistake or retained earnings ends up wrong. Here's a step-by-step look at how the four closing entries actually work, with examples and common mistakes to watch for.


**TLDR:**


- Closing entries move revenue, expenses, and dividends into retained earnings so each period starts at zero.
- Four entries run in a fixed order: close revenue, close expenses, close income summary, then close dividends.
- Always finish adjusting entries before closing. Closing early locks wrong numbers into retained earnings.
- The post-closing trial balance shows only permanent accounts. Any temporary account with a balance signals a missed posting.
- Double automates the month-end close workflow, including journal entry preparation and ledger posting.


## What Are Closing Entries in Accounting


Closing entries are journal entries recorded at the end of an accounting period that move balances from temporary accounts, revenue, expenses, and dividends, into permanent accounts like retained earnings. Each account resets to zero so the next period starts clean instead of carrying forward last period's totals. This step sits after adjusting entries and before the post closing trial balance, closing out the[month-end close process](https://doublehq.com/blog/month-end-close-process-guide/) as every dollar of revenue and expense moves into retained earnings on the balance sheet. Investopedia's overview of[closing entries in accounting](https://www.investopedia.com/terms/c/closing-entry.asp) offers a useful primer if you want to cross-reference the mechanics.


## Temporary vs. Permanent Accounts


Every account on the chart of accounts falls into one of two buckets, and knowing which bucket determines whether it gets touched during closing.


Temporary accounts track activity for a single period only. Revenue, expenses, and dividends or owner withdrawals fall into this group, and each one resets to zero once the period ends.


Permanent accounts carry their balances forward indefinitely. Assets, liabilities, and equity accounts never reset. A cash balance on December 31 becomes the starting cash balance on January 1.


This split exists because income statement accounts measure a period, while balance sheet accounts measure a point in time.


## The Income Summary Account


The income summary account is a temporary holding account that exists only during the closing process. It never appears on the balance sheet or income statement, and it carries no balance outside of closing season. Lumen Learning's[financial accounting chapter on closing entries](https://courses.lumenlearning.com/suny-finaccounting/chapter/journalizing-and-posting-closing-entries/) walks through how this account fits into each step.


Its job is simple: collect every revenue and expense balance in one place before that net figure moves to equity. Revenue accounts close into it as a credit, expense accounts close into it as a debit, and whatever remains is net income or net loss.


That resulting balance then transfers to retained earnings for a corporation, or to the owner's capital account for a sole proprietorship or partnership. Once that transfer posts, the account returns to zero.


## The 4 Closing Entries: Step-by-Step


Closing entries follow the same four-step sequence every time, and the order matters because each step builds on the previous balance.


1. **Close revenue to income summary.** Debit each revenue account for its balance and credit income summary for the total.
2. **Close expenses to income summary.** Credit each expense account and debit income summary, leaving the net result there.
3. **Close income summary to retained earnings.** A credit balance debits income summary and credits retained earnings; a loss reverses the entry.
4. **Close dividends to retained earnings.** Credit dividends and debit retained earnings directly, bypassing income summary entirely.


## Closing Entries Journal Entry Examples and Solutions


Take a small design firm, Maple Creek Design, closing out December with Service Revenue of $48,000, Rent Expense of $12,000, Salaries Expense of $18,000, Utilities Expense of $2,000, and Dividends of $5,000 already paid out. Net income for the period comes to $16,000. Here is how all four entries post.

The first entry wipes out revenue and parks $48,000 on the credit side of income summary. The second wipes out every expense account and lands $32,000 on the debit side of that same account. Net those two together and income summary holds a $16,000 credit balance, which the third entry sweeps into retained earnings. The fourth entry skips income summary entirely: dividends reduce retained earnings directly, since distributions to owners were never part of net income.


## How to Post Closing Entries to the General Ledger


Posting closing entries follows the same mechanics as any journal entry: each debit and credit line moves into its matching account, and[general ledger reconciliation](https://doublehq.com/blog/general-ledger-reconciliation/) confirms the running balance updates line by line as each entry lands.


- Post the revenue to income summary entry first. Revenue zeroes out, and income summary gains a credit line.
- Post each expense closing entry next. Expenses zero out, and income summary picks up an offsetting debit for the total.
- Post the income summary transfer to retained earnings. Income summary nets to zero, and retained earnings reflects net income or net loss.
- Post the dividends closing entry last. Dividends zeroes out, and retained earnings absorbs the reduction.


## Adjusting Entries vs. Closing Entries


Adjusting entries and closing entries solve two different problems, even though both happen at period end and both involve journal entries.


Adjusting entries fix timing. They recognize revenue earned but not yet billed, record[accrued expenses journal entries](https://doublehq.com/blog/accrued-expenses-journal-entry/) for items incurred but not yet paid, or adjust prepaid amounts that have partially expired. These entries post before the financial statements are finalized, since the income statement and balance sheet need to reflect accurate balances first.


Closing entries reset accounts. They run only after those statements are locked in, and their job has nothing to do with accuracy. Revenue and expense balances already reflect the correct period once adjusting entries are done. Closing entries zero those accounts out so next period starts fresh.


The sequence matters: adjust first, report second, close third. Skipping straight to closing without adjusting means the numbers being zeroed out were wrong from the start.


## The Post-Closing Trial Balance


The post-closing trial balance is the final checkpoint of the accounting cycle, run immediately after closing entries post to confirm the ledger is balanced and ready for a new period. Since revenue, expense, and dividend accounts already sit at zero, only permanent accounts show up here: assets, liabilities, and equity, each carrying its ending balance into day one of the next period. Supplies, being an asset, still appears if a balance remains after adjusting entries. Total debits must equal total credits, or an error exists somewhere in the closing process.


## Post-Closing Trial Balance vs. Adjusted Trial Balance


The adjusted trial balance and the post-closing trial balance sit at two different points in the same cycle, and the accounts each one carries mark that difference.

The adjusted version holds revenue and expense figures because the income statement needs them. The post-closing version drops them, since closing entries already moved them into retained earnings. A balance left in either account signals a missed or incorrect posting.


## Common Closing Entry Mistakes and How to Avoid Them


Five mistakes account for most closing errors, each tracing to a specific point in the four-entry sequence.


- Leaving a temporary account open, so its balance carries into the next period instead of resetting to zero, a recurring problem that[accounting automation](https://doublehq.com/blog/accounting-automation-complete-guide/) is designed to prevent.
- Closing a permanent account by mistake, wiping out a balance sheet balance that should carry forward.
- Posting to the wrong period, which distorts both periods at once.
- Closing before accrued items are recorded, leaving income summary with an incomplete number.
- Manual arithmetic errors: research by University of Hawaii professor Ray Panko found 88 to 90 percent of spreadsheets contain at least one error, a core reason firms look into[how to automate the financial close](https://doublehq.com/blog/how-to-automate-financial-close/) .


## Closing Entries Best Practices for a Faster, Cleaner Close


A faster close comes down to sequencing, discipline, and[month-end close automation](https://doublehq.com/blog/month-end-close-automation/) , not shortcuts.


- Set a firm cutoff date. Lock the date after which no new transactions post to the current period. Without one, late invoices or backdated entries slip in after closing has already started, forcing a redo.
- Work from a standardized[month end close checklist](https://doublehq.com/blog/month-end-close-checklist/) . List every account to review, every adjusting entry to confirm, and every closing step in order. A[monthly closing checklist in Excel or PDF](https://doublehq.com/month-end-close-checklist/) keeps the process repeatable across staff and periods instead of depending on memory.
- Finish adjusting entries first. Confirm prepaids, accruals, and[depreciation journal entries](https://doublehq.com/blog/depreciation-journal-entry-guide/) are recorded before touching a single closing entry. Closing early locks in wrong numbers.
- Match every account before transferring balances.[Bank reconciliation](https://doublehq.com/blog/bank-reconciliation-complete-guide-with-examples/) for accounts, credit cards, and control accounts should confirm matches to source documents before revenue and expenses move into income summary.
- Review the post closing trial balance as the final check. Confirm debits equal credits, temporary accounts sit at zero, and only permanent account balances remain before calling the period closed.
